title: Tables, bar graphs and line graphs
blurb: Read two-way tables with the right denominator, read bar heights off any scale, and find the steepest change on a line graph.
question: A campus flu clinic's bar graph shows shots given each weekday: Monday 45, Tuesday 60, Wednesday 35, Thursday 70 and Friday 50. What percent of the week's shots were given on Thursday, and how do you read values like these accurately from the graph?

teach.h: Read the frame before the data
teach.body: Formally, a table or graph is a display that organizes numerical data by category or over time, using labeled axes, units and a scale. In plain English: before you look at a single bar or point, read the title, the axis labels, the units and how much each gridline is worth. Most TEAS graph errors are not math errors at all. They come from reading the wrong row, the wrong series or the wrong scale.

teach.h: Five checks for any table or graph

steps.label: Title
steps.sub: What is being measured, and for whom?

steps.label: Legend
steps.sub: Which color or pattern is which series?

steps.label: Reread the question
steps.sub: Count or percent? Which row? Which time span?

teach.h: A two-way table: health fair volunteers
head: Program
Morning
Afternoon
Total
teach.caption: Each cell counts people in one row AND one column. The totals let you check your reading: 33 + 37 = 70 and 30 + 24 + 16 = 70.

teach.h: Worked example: pick the right denominator
items: Question 1: What percent of the nursing volunteers worked the morning? The group is 'nursing volunteers', so the denominator is the nursing row total, 30.
Question 2: Of the morning volunteers, what fraction were dental students? Now the group is 'morning volunteers', so the denominator is the morning column total, 33.
Question 3: What fraction of ALL volunteers were afternoon pharmacy students? The denominator is the grand total, 70: 15/70 = 3/14.

teach.h: A bar graph: flu shots given each weekday
teach.caption: Bars compare separate categories. The length of each bar is its value, read against the scale.

items: Keisha Brown, a pre-nursing volunteer, must report Thursday's share of the week's flu shots.
Thursday compared with Wednesday: 70 − 35 = 35 more shots, which is 35 ÷ 35 = 100% more (the base is Wednesday, the value you compare FROM).

teach.body: Find the gap between two labeled gridlines, then divide it by the number of equal SPACES (not lines) between them. Labels at 0, 50, 100 with one unlabeled line halfway: each space is 25, so the unlabeled lines sit at 25, 75, 125. A double bar graph has two series side by side; use the legend to match each color to its series before reading anything. Pictographs work the same way: each symbol stands for a stated number, and a half symbol is half that number.

teach.h: A line graph: a patient's temperature over a shift
teach.caption: Line graphs show change over time. The steepest segment is the fastest change: here 1000 to 1200, a rise of 1.4 °F in 2 hours.

items: The readings are equally spaced (2 hours), so the biggest change is the fastest: 1000 to 1200.
Rate of change = change ÷ time = 1.4 ÷ 2 = 0.7 °F per hour. Check: 0.7 × 2 = 1.4. ✓
If the time gaps are NOT equal, divide each change by its own time gap before comparing.

teach.text: Classic slips: counting gridlines as 1 each when they are worth 25; using the grand total when the question says 'of the morning volunteers'; reporting a count when a percent is asked; and picking the biggest change on a line graph without dividing by unequal time gaps.

items: Read title, labels, units, scale and legend before any data.
Two-way tables: the phrase after 'of the...' names the denominator (a row or column total).
Bar graphs compare categories; each gridline gap ÷ number of spaces = value per space.
Line graphs show change over time; steepest segment = greatest rate of change (change ÷ time).

summary: You can now read two-way tables using the correct row, column or grand total as the denominator, read bar heights off any scale, and find and calculate the fastest change on a line graph. You also know the scale, legend and count-versus-percent slips the TEAS uses as distractors.

A.q: A survey of 200 pre-nursing students records commute by class year. Walk: 22 freshmen, 18 sophomores. Drive: 36 freshmen, 54 sophomores. Bus: 42 freshmen, 28 sophomores. Of the students who drive, what percent are sophomores?
A.why: The group is 'students who drive', so the denominator is the drive row total: 36 + 54 = 90. Sophomores who drive: 54. 54 ÷ 90 = 0.6 = 60%.

whyNot.0: 54 ÷ 200 = 27% uses the whole survey as the denominator, not just the drivers.
whyNot.1: 36 ÷ 90 = 40% is the freshman share of drivers: the wrong cell in the row.
whyNot.2: 54 ÷ 100 = 54% uses the sophomore column total, which answers 'what percent of sophomores drive'.

A.q: A bar graph of weekly clinic visits has its vertical axis labeled at 0, 50, 100, 150 and 200, with one unlabeled gridline halfway between each pair of labels. The Week 3 bar ends on the second unlabeled gridline above 0, and the Week 4 bar ends at the 150 label. How many visits were there in Weeks 3 and 4 combined?
A.why: Each space is 50 ÷ 2 = 25, so the unlabeled lines are at 25, 75, 125 and 175. The second unlabeled line above 0 is 75. 75 + 150 = 225.

whyNot.0: This reads Week 3 as 25, the first unlabeled gridline, not the second.
whyNot.1: This reads Week 3 as 50, counting the second gridline of any kind instead of the second unlabeled one.
whyNot.3: This reads Week 3 as 100, the second labeled gridline.

A.q: A line graph shows a patient's systolic blood pressure, in mm Hg: 0800: 152; 0900: 145; 1200: 130; 1300: 124; 1600: 118. Between which two consecutive readings did the pressure fall at the fastest rate?
A.why: Divide each drop by its time gap: 7 ÷ 1 = 7 per hour; 15 ÷ 3 = 5 per hour; 6 ÷ 1 = 6 per hour; 6 ÷ 3 = 2 per hour. The fastest fall is 0800 to 0900.

whyNot.1: This is the largest total drop (15 mm Hg), but it took 3 hours: only 5 mm Hg per hour.
whyNot.2: This drop is 6 mm Hg in 1 hour, slower than the 7 mm Hg per hour from 0800 to 0900.
whyNot.3: This segment holds the lowest readings, but its drop is only 2 mm Hg per hour.

B.q: A double bar graph shows flu immunization rates at four clinics. Blue bars are 2023 and gray bars are 2024. Clinic A: blue 72%, gray 81%. Clinic B: blue 88%, gray 84%. Clinic C: blue 65%, gray 77%. Clinic D: blue 90%, gray 93%. Which clinic had the greatest increase from 2023 to 2024?
B.why: Gray minus blue: A +9, B −4, C +12, D +3 percentage points. Clinic C rose the most.

whyNot.0: Clinic A rose 9 points, less than Clinic C's 12.
whyNot.1: Clinic B fell 4 points. It only looks like a rise if the legend colors are swapped.
whyNot.3: Clinic D has the tallest 2024 bar, but it rose just 3 points.

B.q: A table lists one clinic's 800 visits by insurance type: Private 312, Medicare 228, Medicaid 180, Uninsured 80. What percent of all visits were covered by Medicare or Medicaid? Round to the nearest tenth of a percent.

whyNot.2: 49.0% is the complement: Private plus Uninsured (392 ÷ 800).

B.q: A line graph shows a child's height: age 2, 34 inches; age 4, 40 inches; age 6, 45 inches; age 8, 50 inches. What was the average rate of growth from age 2 to age 8, in inches per year? Round to the nearest tenth.
B.why: Rate of change = change in height ÷ change in age = (50 − 34) ÷ (8 − 2) = 16 ÷ 6 = 2.67, which rounds to 2.7 inches per year.

whyNot.0: 16 ÷ 8 = 2.0 divides by the final age instead of the 6 years that passed.
whyNot.2: 16 ÷ 3 = 5.3 divides by the number of gaps between plotted points, not the number of years.
whyNot.3: 50 ÷ 8 = 6.3 divides one reading by one age instead of change by change.

C.q: A hospital's line graph shows monthly flu admissions: October 40, November 70, December 112, January 140, February 98. Which month-to-month change was the greatest percent increase?
C.why: Percent increase = change ÷ starting month. Oct to Nov: 30 ÷ 40 = 75%. Nov to Dec: 42 ÷ 70 = 60%. Dec to Jan: 28 ÷ 112 = 25%. October to November is greatest.

whyNot.1: This is the largest increase in admissions (42), but from a bigger base it is only 60%.
whyNot.3: Admissions fell from 140 to 98, a 30% decrease.

C.q: In a pictograph of vaccinations, each syringe symbol represents 40 vaccinations. Thursday's row shows 6 full symbols and one half symbol. How many vaccinations does Thursday's row represent?
C.why: 6 full symbols = 6 × 40 = 240. A half symbol = 40 ÷ 2 = 20. Total 240 + 20 = 260.

whyNot.1: 250 counts the half symbol as 10, a quarter of 40 instead of half.
whyNot.3: 280 counts the half symbol as a full one (7 × 40).

C.q: A bar graph shows a clinic's missed appointments: January 80, February 68, March 51. By what percent did missed appointments fall from January to March? Round to the nearest tenth of a percent.
C.why: Percent change = (new − original) ÷ original = (51 − 80) ÷ 80 = −29 ÷ 80 = −0.3625, a 36.3% decrease.

whyNot.0: 29 is the drop in appointments, a count, not a percent.
whyNot.2: 40% adds the monthly changes (15% then 25%). Successive percents cannot be added.
whyNot.3: 29 ÷ 51 = 56.9% divides by the new value instead of the original.

reteach.title: A graph is a map of the numbers
reteach.question: Before a road trip you check a map's legend and its scale bar, or '1 inch = 10 miles' could become '1 inch = 1 mile.' How does the same habit stop graph errors?

blocks.body: On a map you check the legend (what the symbols mean), the scale bar (how far one inch really is) and where you are going. A graph is the same. The legend tells you which bar or line is which series, the gridlines are the scale bar, and the question is the destination. Measure the route with the wrong scale and every distance is wrong, even if your arithmetic is perfect.

blocks.text: Gridline gap ÷ number of SPACES, not lines. Labels 0 and 30 with two unlabeled lines between them make three spaces of 10, so the lines sit at 10 and 20.

explain.body: Take the gap between two labeled gridlines and divide it by the number of equal spaces between them. That gives the value of each unlabeled line. Never assume each line is worth 1.

explain.caption: Two lines make three spaces: 30 ÷ 3 = 10 per space.

test.q: A line graph's vertical axis is labeled 0, 30, 60 and 90, with two evenly spaced unlabeled gridlines between each pair of labels. A point sits on the second unlabeled gridline above 60. What value does it show?
test.why: Two unlabeled lines make three equal spaces: 30 ÷ 3 = 10. The lines above 60 are at 70 and 80, so the second one is 80.

whyNot.1: 70 is the first unlabeled gridline above 60, not the second.
whyNot.2: 75 divides the 30-unit gap into 4 spaces instead of 3.

explain.body: Each cell belongs to one row and one column. For 'of the X, what percent...' questions, X is your denominator: a row total, a column total or the grand total. Find X first, then the cell.

test.q: Using the table of 120 clinic patients (adults: 45 vaccinated, 15 not; children: 50 vaccinated, 10 not), what percent of the children are not vaccinated? Round to the nearest tenth of a percent.
test.why: 'Of the children' sets the denominator as the children's total, 60. Unvaccinated children: 10. 10 ÷ 60 = 0.1667 = 16.7%.

whyNot.0: 10 ÷ 120 = 8.3% uses the grand total as the denominator.
whyNot.2: 10 ÷ 25 = 40% answers 'what percent of unvaccinated patients are children'.
whyNot.3: 50 ÷ 60 = 83.3% is the percent of children who ARE vaccinated.

explain.body: Bar graphs compare separate categories. A double bar graph puts two series side by side, so match each color or pattern to the legend before reading. Swapping the series flips every comparison.

test.q: A double bar graph shows average hours of sleep. Solid bars are weeknights and striped bars are weekends. Jordan: solid 6, striped 9. Priya: solid 7, striped 8. Luis: solid 5.5, striped 9.5. Ana: solid 8, striped 7.5. Whose weekend sleep exceeds weeknight sleep by the most?
test.why: Striped minus solid: Jordan 3, Priya 1, Luis 4, Ana −0.5. Luis has the largest difference.

whyNot.1: Jordan's difference is 3 hours, less than Luis's 4.
whyNot.2: Ana sleeps less on weekends. She only comes out on top if the solid and striped series are swapped.

explain.h: Line graphs and rate of change
explain.body: A line graph shows change over time. Rate of change = change in value ÷ change in time. Convert times carefully: 0600 to 0830 is 2 hours 30 minutes, which is 2.5 hours.

test.q: A line graph shows an IV bag holding 1,000 mL at 0600 and 700 mL at 0830, falling at a steady rate. At what rate did the volume decrease?

whyNot.3: 700 ÷ 2.5 = 280 divides the volume remaining instead of the change.
